title: When And How To Teach Your Classroom Management Plan
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a boundary-setting script for teachers being pressured by a bossy colleague, arguing that the entire problem can be solved with one repeated, calmly delivered phrase: 'No, I'm not going to do that.' He walks through the mechanics of the interaction -- offering a brief, non-defensive reason if pressed ('it's a good idea, but not right for me'), redirecting the conversation, and refusing to over-explain or apologize -- while acknowledging it takes real courage, especially with colleagues who have long been in a position of influence. He frames the payoff not just as relief from a specific annoyance but as a shift in how that colleague and others perceive the teacher, from someone who can be pressured into anything to a competent, independent professional. The piece closes by pairing firmness with continued warmth, arguing that boundary-setting and basic collegiality aren't in conflict.
points: A single calm, repeated phrase -- 'No, I'm not going to do that' -- is offered as sufficient to stop a pressuring colleague after one or two repetitions.
If pressed for a reason, a brief non-explanation like 'it's a good idea, but not right for me' is enough; extended justification undermines the boundary.
Setting the boundary firmly does not require coldness afterward; staying warm and friendly in daily interactions is presented as compatible with firmness.
Standing up to a bossy colleague is framed as necessary for professional survival, since chronic appeasement is identified as a path toward quitting teaching.
quotes: It’s to calmly and respectfully repeat the same phrase whenever they begin pressuring you to do (or teach) anything you don’t want to do.
Now, if they follow up by asking why not, just say “It’s a good idea, but not right for me.” There is no need to go on and on or explain further.
You have to stand up for yourself in this profession to avoid the kind of stress that will cause you to quit teaching.
They’ll begin to view you as a strong, independent, and competent teacher who doesn’t need their constant input.
But always, with everyone, maintain and defend your personal and professional boundaries.
